newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-Comics craze conquers Hong Kong hearts.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Comics craze conquers Hong Kong hearts.

text.p: A comics craze is sweeping through Hong Kong, dominating the lives of thousands of fanatics willing to brave the elements and even do combat for a good, vulgar read.

"I came to queue at 10 o'clock last night," said Paul, one of some 1,500 young comic fanatics who camped overnight outside a recent book fair, getting set to rush in and snap up the pick of comics on the opening day.
The fresh college graduate forked out HK$2,000 (US$258) on original comics, plus more than HK$6,000 on comic books and related items at the show whose main appeal was comics.

Hong Kong is a small territory of 6.4 million people within China, but huge crowds and queues are quickly whipped up by hobbyists and collectors pouncing on a speculative good buy -- from comics to new issues of stamps, and coins.
COMIC CRAZE FUELLED BY COLLECTOR'S VALUE
"The value of the originals are set to appreciate greatly," he enthused, although he said he would never sell his favourites.
Frenzied youths rushed to comic stalls to snap up limited editions. Some jumped the queue or were pushed over the barricades in a chaos that called for police to keep order.
Comic fans who could not wait to read their favourite books plonked themselves down on the floor in a corner to devour their spiritual food right away.
"At the more popular stalls, you have to queue up for at least half an hour before you can buy," said one teenage boy who queued all night outside the exhibition hall.
"If you go to every one of them, you need to spend hours queuing alone," he said. "Comic books in limited editions will be sold out in a minute!" he exclaimed.
Such overwhelming fervour forced some comic fanatics to arrange a strategic division of labour with like-minded friends. They would buy at different stalls for later swaps.
"The crowd was formidable," a marketing agent at a comic publisher said of the huge turnout. "Some titles are already sold out now," he said. "Reading comics has become a trend.
HONG KONG FEEDS ON COMICS FROM KUNG FU TO THE SURREAL
Hong Kong, with a comics market turnover estimated at more than HK$800 million a year, sports a wide assortment of comics.
Themes range from Chinese martial arts and Chinese classic fiction to detective stories and the surreal. Some feature sex and violence, which has led to controversy.
They include local creations and Japanese titles, with the latter increasingly stealing the show.
JAPANESE THEMES ARE ALL THE RAGE
Some youths read several comic books every day.
"I love reading comics. I'm very fond of Dragon Ball, for example," said 12-year-old Lam Man-hon.

Dragon Ball, a Japanese title which is one of the best sellers and shown in a televised cartoon, depicts quests by goodies and baddies for seven dragon balls and involves a "dragon god" who makes wishes come true.
"I like comics because the drawings are pretty," said 11-year-old Kevin Chow. "I like detective comics. I can finish reading a comic book in half an hour."
Nineteen-year-old student Esther Chung was never frugal with comics. "I spend more than HK$200 on comics a month. But a friend of mine reads seven to eight comic books every week."
PLEASE DO NOT DISTURB -- COMIC READERS AT WORK
Teenager Tom was so absorbed in his reading that he was annoyed at being interrupted by a reporter.
"Hush!," he whispered, holding out his arm in a "no interruption" sign, as all his attention was gripped by a comic book depicting fighting and violence.
"When I see a comic book that I like, I buy it right away," Tom said after he had finished a page.
Many working adults are just as besotted, it seems.
"I'm taking a day off just to come to this book fair," said a man in his thirties. Many grown-ups read comics while queuing, waiting or commuting.

Japanese comics are becoming ever more popular. Fans like the quality of their drawing and the diversity of themes. Their popularity is also backed up by television cartoons portraying the same stories.
The mainstay of local comics are martial arts heroes who fight for good against evil. Stories starring late kung fu legend Bruce Lee still abound 24 years after his death.
